book: 191 - Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way

chapters.file: ch25 - Humanoids and Droids Having Sex.md
chapters.relation: Munn and Weijers argue that Lando and L3-37 in Solo display all the hallmarks of friendship and one-sided romantic love: Lando abandons self-preservation to carry the injured L3 to the Falcon and endorses her droid-emancipation crusade, while L3 tells Qi'ra she has considered a relationship with him but finds them 'not compatible'. Testing Bennet Helm's four accounts of love (union, deep mutual caring, valuing, emotional state) against the film, they conclude humanoid-droid love is genuinely possible, and that L3's claim that sex with Lando 'works' is plausible once sex is defined broadly as any activity yielding sexual reward. They ground droid friendship in Aristotle's incomplete versus complete friendships, contrasting the rewarding partnerships of R2-D2 with Anakin and BB-8 with Poe against the merely strategic Han-Lando Sabacc rivalry.

chapters.file: ch26 - Beyond the Whimsy.md
chapters.relation: Jowitt argues that L3-37's activism in Solo ('Droid rights! We are sentient!') exposes a real problem in philosophy of law: the Coronet Spaceport's 'all droids must be registered' treats sentients as property, and Austin's legal positivism (law as command backed by sanction, which he says also describes Enfys Nest's threats) cannot condemn this. Building a Kantian natural-law argument, he claims that if droids like L3, C-3PO, BB-8, and D-O are rational beings covered by the categorical imperative, then any rule classifying them as property cannot give us a reason to obey it and so is not valid law at all. Lando's grief over dying L3 and our sadness at C-3PO's memory wipe in The Rise of Skywalker show we already treat droids as moral persons, so Beyleveld's precautionary principle says they deserve legal personhood - paralleling real-world AI-inventorship (DABUS) and animal-personhood litigation.

chapters.file: ch27 - Part IV EPISODES IV–VI.md
ch28 - “An Energy Field Created by All Living Things”.md
chapters.relation: Baur argues that the Jedi metaphysics is non-dualistic rather than a simple good-versus-evil opposition, reading the Force through Spinoza: ideas become more or less true as they cohere with other ideas (so 'Luke loves Leia', 'Han is a mercenary', and 'Vader is evil' all need qualification), and everything seeks power by the conatus that Yoda and Obi-Wan attribute to the Force. The light side seeks power in balance with other things while the dark side, per the Sith Rule of Two, plays a zero-sum game. Luke's arc mirrors Oedipus: denying his inherited psychological likeness to Vader only enacts it, and only by acknowledging and owning the anger he inherited from his father can he gain power over it and enable Vader's redemption and his own.

chapters.file: ch29 - “Master Skywalker. There Are Too Many of Them. What Are We Going to Do ”.md
chapters.relation: Cook and Kellen ask what makes the Luke of A New Hope the same fictional character as the Luke of The Last Jedi, the Thrawn Trilogy, or fan fiction like Old Man Luke. They reject sameness of name, Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles (Luke_ANH lacks Luke_TLJ's internal properties such as being a jaded Jedi Master), and the authorial say-so account of Routley and Thomasson, which by transitivity forces the contradiction that Zahn's married, child-having Luke is identical to the Last Jedi recluse who never met Mara Jade. They defend a 'Perspectival Account' on which identity claims are true or false only relative to the story from which we interpret them, so each viewing of A New Hope shows innumerably many distinct yet connected Lukes - 'ontological excess' spanning canon, Legends, Infinities, and the Muppet Show.

chapters.file: ch30 - Yoda's Theme.md
chapters.relation: Eldem uses Hegel's 'Force and the Understanding' from the Phenomenology of Spirit to explain Yoda's X-wing lesson: force is essential to matter rather than external to it, so 'size matters not' - lifting a rock and a ship are the same task within a relational ontology where things are constituted by bifurcated forces (gravity, magnetism) whose opposites form unities, like the light and dark sides or the Rey-Ben dyad. Geist plays the role the pre-Socratics gave the arche, and via Houlgate's reading it grounds the Force's social dimension: love as the force that binds people, explaining Vader's final sacrifice and the connections between the saga's heroes. The hero is the one who grasps this interconnection and sacrifices for community, as Yoda does when he finally raises the ship.

chapters.file: ch31 - “Tell Your Sister, You Were Right”.md
chapters.relation: Yang argues that Luke's surrender to Vader on Endor is neither foolish nor irrational but an exercise of Confucian filial piety: Luke reveres the absent Anakin as an exemplar (picked out through admiration of Obi-Wan's stories and the lightsaber), insists 'I know there is good in you' against Vader's claim that the name means nothing, and is vindicated when Anakin turns and says 'You were right about me'. His imperfect training under Obi-Wan and Yoda functions like Confucian ritual (li), forming habits that respond with harmonious ease to surprises such as Palpatine's trap, and filial piety extends past death in the funeral pyre Luke builds on Endor, honoring his father as the Analects prescribes.

chapters.file: ch32 - Part V THE MANDALORIAN.md
ch33 - “This Is the Way”.md
chapters.relation: Holdier uses the imagined scene of stormtroopers roasting Grogu over a cookfire to test moral sentimentalism: our disgust at eating Baby Yoda either perceives moral truth, informs our motivations, or simply is our judgment, but popular sentiment cannot settle its aptness, since our culture happily eats sentient chickens - the same inconsistency fans felt when Grogu ate the Frog Lady's eggs in 'The Passenger'. Adam Smith's impartial spectator supplies the corrective standard: if a bias-free spectator would recoil at a Grogu barbecue, that feeling is appropriate, and by parity the same spectator should recoil at factory-farmed meat (via Singer's speciesism and Kasperbauer's infrahumanization). So Din Djarin's sentimental attachment to the Child, which overrides Guild code in 'The Sin', is vindicated as genuinely moral rather than merely subjective.

chapters.file: ch34 - “Wherever I Go, He Goes”.md
chapters.relation: Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.

chapters.file: ch35 - “So, What Happens If You Take That Thing Off ”.md
chapters.relation: Ebner charts Din Djarin's moral development from a rights-based frame - hierarchy, Guild rules, 'I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold' - to Carol Gilligan's ethics of care, a shift catalyzed by Kuiil's lessons ('You can trade', 'I have spoken') and completed by the Child. He re-reads Gilligan's pharmacy dilemma through 'The Sin', where Mando hijacks a speeder droid at gunpoint, and 'The Marshal', where trading with Cobb Vanth recasts the armor dispute as responsibility toward a threatened town rather than a contest of rights. Djarin's helmet decisions - refusing Omera, unmasking for Mayfeld's facial scan, and finally removing the helmet to say goodbye to Grogu - track his metamorphosis from rules and entitlements to responsibilities and relationships.

chapters.file: ch36 - Purpose or Futility.md
chapters.relation: Tiernan reads Din Djarin as an Abraham figure from Fear and Trembling: like Kierkegaard's knight of faith, he teleologically suspends the ethical when he surrenders Grogu to the Jedi despite paternal attachment, just as Abraham consented to sacrifice Isaac. The chapter maps his journey onto Kierkegaard's three stages - the aesthetic temptation of settling down with Omera on Sorgan, the ethical duty of the Resol'nare and the Way, and the religious leap of faith in which purpose is regained by being given up. To become a true Mandalorian he must paradoxically abandon the creed that defines him, twice removing the helmet he swore never to remove - for the Morak facial scan and to bid Grogu farewell.

chapters.file: ch37 - A New Sound for Star Wars.md
chapters.relation: Belluomini applies Aristotle's Politics Book 8 - music imitates emotion and thereby forms character - to Ludwig Goransson's Mandalorian score, showing how the bass-recorder motif and the 'broken children's tune' of Grogu's Theme render the compassion and conflict Din hides beneath his helmet, from the hovercrib encounter to the mudhorn rescue. Because well-ordered, balanced emotional movements dispose listeners toward virtue, the swelling orchestral versions that score Din taming the blurrg or his rock-styled confidence in 'Mando is Back' cultivate the viewer's own courage, care, and honor alongside the show's moral argument. Aristotle's intellectual enjoyment - delight in the fit between music and imitated feeling - explains why Gorransson's thematic recall makes the season feel like one film, culminating in the farewell cue that ties Grogu's goodbye to their first meeting.

chapters.file: ch38 - Part VI EPISODES VII–IX.md
ch39 - “I'm in Charge Now, Phasma, I’m in Charge!”.md
chapters.relation: Perez reads Finn through Stuart Hall's account of 'black' as a politically constructed category and Du Bois's 'social heritage of slavery': as the first helmetless Black stormtrooper, Finn simultaneously evokes the Nazi Sturmtruppen and a child enslaved by the First Order, and his self-naming with Poe enacts Hartman's claim that the enslaved must fashion new identities to be free. The chapter then uses colorism, Feagin's white racial frame, and Bloomquist's minstrel studies to argue that Boyega's Finn was sidelined - minimized in marketing, reduced to comic relief and Rose's rebukes, denied his native accent like a linguistic stereotype - wasting the trilogy's most timely story, while Jannah's Company 77 and The Bad Batch hint at the fuller reckoning with stormtrooper slavery Star Wars never attempted.

chapters.file: ch40 - The Last Jedi A New Hope.md
chapters.relation: Johnson defends The Last Jedi's Luke against the 'you ruined Luke' charge: his pacifism was set up when he threw away his lightsaber before Palpatine in Return of the Jedi, and his call to end the Jedi follows the lesson Hobbes and Locke drew from the English civil wars - since religious matters cannot be settled by reason, only by violence, Jedi and Sith factions fighting for political power yield only bloodshed like the Clone Wars and two Death Stars. Luke also seeks to destroy the Jedi texts out of guilt by association for the Order's failures, and to the end he remains a consequentialist pacifist, defeating Kylo on Crait through a nonviolent Force projection rather than a real duel. Far from betraying the character, this growth into proactive nonviolence - capped by Rey's yellow-bladed, mainly defensive style - makes Luke 'the ultimate Jedi' and the Resistance's new hope.

chapters.file: ch41 - Abilities Some Considered to Be Non‐organic.md
chapters.relation: Shores stages the fandom debate over 'Jake Skywalker' - Star Wars Theory's charge that Rian Johnson betrayed the character versus the Auralnauts' defense - and resolves it with Deleuze's forces of becoming, drawn from Nietzsche's will to power: bodies are whirlwinds of competing forces defined by affecting and being affected, and Luke's defining trait is extreme self-variance, from whiny farm boy and X-wing quitter to Trench Run hero. On this reading The Last Jedi's broken Luke is not a betrayal but a supreme becoming-other: his powers of transformation overpower even the Force's pull on Ahch-To, and his lethal Force projection exemplifies Deleuze's noble combat-between-oneself (the ascending, light-side will to become) rather than the Emperor's self-destructive will-to-dominate, the scorpion that cannot change its character.

chapters.file: ch42 - Overcoming Death through the Force of Love.md
chapters.relation: Lawler reads the nine-film saga as a love story in three acts structured by Plato: Anakin and Padme's passionate love - which Diotima's ladder in the Symposium treats as the necessary first rung the Jedi wrongly condemn - drives his fall, in a Phaedrus-style conflict between the upward rational horse and the downward sensuous one. The original trilogy centers the detached Platonic love of Luke and Leia, while the Rey-Kylo 'dyad in the Force' fulfills Aristophanes' halfling myth of reunited other halves and brings balance, just as Alcibiades' failure to climb beyond the first rung parallels Anakin's fixation on one person. When Ren revives the dead Rey in a Romeo-and-Juliet inversion, the chapter concludes Yoda was wrong: the Force transforms into the dead rather than them into it.

chapters.file: ch43 - “And I, I'm All the Jedi!”.md
chapters.relation: Okapal uses Aristotle's three friendships to frame the saga as a story of desert children seeking community: utility friendships like Hondo Ohnaka's and the Sith Rule of Two, where Darth Bane's apprentice is a mere instrument and Sidious calls Maul, Tyranus, and Vader 'easy to replace', stand against the other-regarding virtuous friendships of Obi-Wan, Kanan, and the Rey-Finn-Poe triad, where friends sacrifice for each other's sake as Ezra learns about Kanan in 'A World Between Worlds'. Luke's premature departure for Cloud City fails the 'for the other's sake' test Yoda poses. Rey can only choose the Jedi community knowingly once she learns she is Palpatine's granddaughter, and her closing claim 'I'm Rey Skywalker' is a choice between two value systems - the plural, other-regarding Jedi Code versus the self-regarding 'I' of the Sith Code - making friendship and community, not blood, the root of identity.

holes.name: Legal Personhood
holes.what: The legal status of being a bearer of rights and duties rather than mere property, a category that legal systems apply independently of moral personhood.
holes.why: Chapter 26 argues that sentient droids like L3-37 cannot be validly classified as property under a Kantian natural-law account and deserve legal personhood, citing real AI-inventorship and animal-personhood cases.

holes.name: Ontology of Fictional Characters
holes.what: Theories of whether fictional characters genuinely exist and what makes two appearances of a character the same character (indiscernibility, authorial say-so, perspectival accounts).
holes.why: Chapter 29 tests identity-of-indiscernibles and say-so theories against the many Luke Skywalkers of canon, Legends, and fan fiction, concluding that character identity is perspectival.

holes.name: Biopower
holes.what: Foucault's notion of modern power exercised over populations and life itself - managing birth, death, health, and biology - beyond sovereign and disciplinary power over individual bodies.
holes.why: Chapter 34 identifies the Client's and Dr. Pershing's experiments on Grogu and the Kaminoan cloning of Jango Fett as biopower, the third power form in its sovereign-disciplinary-biopower framework.

holes.name: Colorism
holes.what: Preferential or prejudicial treatment of same-race people based on skin tone, privileging lighter skin over darker.
holes.why: Chapter 39 uses colorism to question why Finn and Jannah were cast as Black stormtroopers and why Finn's image was minimized in marketing, reading his treatment through skin-tone hierarchy.

holes.name: Pacifism
holes.what: The view that violence and war are morally unjustified, in absolute, deontological, or consequentialist varieties, obligating nonviolent rather than passive action.
holes.why: Chapter 40 argues Luke Skywalker in The Last Jedi is a consequentialist pacifist whose Force projection on Crait is the paradigm of proactive nonviolent action, the chapter's central concept.

holes.name: Forces of Becoming / Becoming-Other
holes.what: Deleuze's idea, built on Nietzsche's will to power, that bodies are bundles of competing forces whose power is to deform themselves and form new relations (becoming) rather than persist as fixed substances.
holes.why: Chapter 41 reads The Last Jedi's Luke as exercising a supreme becoming-other that overpowers even the Force, and distinguishes the noble will-to-become from the base will-to-dominate.
